qs.e: Gluteus maximus is the largest muscle in the body and plays a crucial role in hip extension, particularly when rising from a seated position or climbing stairs. It is innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve.

qs.q: The gluteus maximus muscle is primarily responsible for which action at the hip joint?
qs.e: The gluteus maximus is the strongest muscle of the hip, primarily responsible for extension and powerful lateral rotation of the hip joint. It is crucial for standing up from a seated position and climbing stairs.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Anatomy Exam - May 22, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The gluteus maximus is the largest buttock muscle, responsible for hip extension and external rotation. It is key for standing, walking, and climbing stairs.

sections.p: A thick, superficial muscle covering the posterior hip, forming the bulk of the buttock.
b: Largest skeletal muscle in the body

sections.p: Originates from the ilium, sacrum, coccyx, and thoracolumbar fascia; inserts into the iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosity of the femur.
b: Insertion via IT band transmits force to the knee

sections.p: Superficial to the gluteus medius and minimus; deep to the subcutaneous fat and skin; overlies the sciatic nerve in the gluteal region.
b: Sciatic nerve runs beneath the muscle

sections.p: Primarily from the inferior gluteal artery, with contributions from the superior gluteal artery.
b: Inferior gluteal artery supplies lower fibers
Superior gluteal artery supplies upper fibers

t.b: Assess arterial patency when ischemic buttock pain suspected; absent flow suggests vascular injury

sections.p: Innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve (L5‑S2).

t.b: Detects inferior gluteal nerve injury; reduced motor unit potentials indicate neuropathy

sections.p: Extends and laterally rotates the hip; stabilises the pelvis during gait; assists in rising from a seated position.
Weakness or injury can cause gait disturbances, lower back pain, and difficulty rising. Overuse may lead to gluteal tendinopathy; trauma can cause avulsion fractures.
b: Inferior gluteal nerve palsy → hip extension weakness
Avulsion fracture in adolescents after forceful hip extension

t.b: If MRI unavailable, use bedside ultrasound to detect large tears
Assesses hip extension strength; inability suggests gluteus maximus weakness

sections.p: During physical exam, ask the patient to rise from a seated position and extend the hip against resistance to test strength.
b: Hip extension against resistance evaluates gluteus maximus
Observe for asymmetry of buttock bulk

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of hip extension after trauma (possible nerve injury or fracture)
Severe buttock pain with fever (possible deep infection or abscess)
Rapidly expanding gluteal swelling causing neurovascular compromise

faq.q: Why is the inferior gluteal nerve more important than the superior gluteal nerve for this muscle?
faq.a: The inferior gluteal nerve provides the motor supply to gluteus maximus; the superior gluteal nerve supplies the more superficial gluteal muscles.

faq.q: Can a gluteal injection damage the gluteus maximus?
faq.a: If injected too low, it can injure the sciatic nerve; proper upper‑outer quadrant avoids muscle damage and nerve injury.

faq.q: What posture problem can result from chronic gluteus maximus weakness?
faq.a: Weakness leads to anterior pelvic tilt and low back pain due to loss of posterior pelvic support.
